newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE - What caused Colombia's recession?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - What caused Colombia's recession?.

text.p: Colombia's billionaire cocaine merchants have been blamed for many of the country's problems, including endemic corruption, violence and its reputation as a "narco-democracy."

But few here are willing to accept the government's claim that "withdrawal symptoms" -- and efforts to break Colombia's long dependency on drug dollars -- helped spark the recession that Colombia slid into in the first quarter of 1997.

President Ernesto Samper has said repeatedly that his administration's crackdown on the Cali drug cartel was a leading cause of growing unemployment and the fall in economic growth which Colombia posted in the final quarter of 1996 and the first three months of this year.

With all of its top drug lords either dead or in jail, Colombia is no longer getting the billions of dollars in cocaine cash that entered the country every year, Samper and other government officials have said, referring proudly to the government's so-called "ethical adjustment" of the economy.
STILL HOOKED ON "EASY MONEY"

U.S. officials insist that Cali cartel's bosses continue to run their criminal empire from inside the maximum security wing of Bogota's Picota prison, however. And the country's booming trade in contraband goods, which industrialists blame for a sharp slowdown in the manufacturing sector, belies the argument that Colombia has broken its dependency on "easy money."

The trade in contraband, with top items ranging from Scotch whisky and Marlboro cigarettes to Japanese TV sets and U.S-made refrigerators, is valued at billions a year and drug experts say it is the leading form of laundering illicit proceeds from Colombia's narcotics sales abroad.

Underscoring the view of Colombia as a country where criminal drug syndicates continue to wield considerable clout, a survey in Newsweek magazine ranked it, along with Guatemala and worse even then Russia, as the country most infected by organised crime.

The survey, overseen by respected Harvard economist Jeffrey Sachs and conducted under the auspices of the World Economic Forum, also described Colombia as the world's "most problematic" country in terms of tax evasion and ranked it 41st on a list of 53 nations in terms of overall competitiveness.
STATE OF NATIONAL PESSIMISM

Samper's government conceded for the first time on May 29 that Colombia was in the grip of recession. But even before that, opposition politicians and business leaders had begun to refer to a state of "national pessimism."

Apart from concern over Colombia's dismal economic performance last year, when economic growth fell to 2.1 percent from a 3.7 percent annual average since 1980, that pessimism has been fuelled by a resurgence in guerrilla violence, rocky relations with Washington, Colombia's main trading partner, and the fact that government officials say 90 percent of all crimes go unpunished in Colombia -- a country with the highest kidnapping and murder rates in Latin America.
Stephen Edkins, a Bogota-based analyst with Santander Investment, said most of the pessimism in Colombia "is probably being overdone," at least in terms of the economy.

Edkins, who acknowledges seeing "a little bit of a lie" in the government's talk about the economic effects of cracking down on drug lords, said :"Colombia is going through historically low rates of growth."
But he stressed that "international investors remain very confident" in Colombia and said he sees it posting positive year-on-year growth despite the bad start to 1997.
"We've already touched bottom," Edkins said.
WORSE YET TO COME?

Armando Montenegro, a leading critic of government economic policy and of what former finance minister Rudolf Hommes describes as the Samper administration's "neo-incompetence," is less confident about the future, however.

Montenegro, who heads the respected National Association of Financial Institutions, predicted gross domestic product would be flat in the second quarter of this year and said there would only be a return to weak positive growth in the second half of the year.

"The situation in most sectors isn't showing any improvement as the days go by," he told Reuters, adding that most of what the government has said about the "ethical adjustment" was nothing but "official propaganda."
Political uncertainty, the government's constant flip- flopping on economic policy, and the recent appreciation of the peso currency, were among the leading causes of the recession, Montenegro said.

He added that the advent of presidential elections next year -- in which Horacio Serpa, Samper's populist former interior minister and right-hand man promises to be a leading contender -- threatened to make matters even worse because "businessmen are very afraid of where the country is heading."

Whether or not Colombia manages to pull out of recession, respected Inter-American Development Bank economist Eduardo Lora says the country has lost something crucial -- its long-term reputation for prudent economic policy and growth.

In the 1980s, Colombia was considered the most stable economy in Latin America, Lora said in an interview with Bogota's El Espectador newspaper. "In the 90s, it dropped from first to fifth place in terms of stability and growth, and in the last two years it has fallen to No. 11," he said.
